claim: Large Ca transients cause massive endocytosis (MEND) in BHK fibroblasts by nonclassical mechanisms.
source: Large Ca transients cause massive endocytosis (MEND) in BHK fibroblasts by nonclassical mechanisms.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a primary finding of the study.

claim: MEND depends on mitochondrial permeability transition pore (PTP) openings.
source: We present evidence that MEND depends on mitochondrial permeability transition pore (PTP) openings, followed by coenzyme A (CoA) release, acyl CoA synthesis, and membrane protein palmitoylation.
evidence: The abstract presents this as evidence from the study, supported by experimental data in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: MEND is followed by coenzyme A (CoA) release from mitochondria.
source: We present evidence that MEND depends on mitochondrial permeability transition pore (PTP) openings, followed by coenzyme A (CoA) release, acyl CoA synthesis, and membrane protein palmitoylation.
evidence: The abstract presents this as part of the sequential pathway leading to MEND.

claim: MEND requires acyl CoA synthesis.
source: We present evidence that MEND depends on mitochondrial permeability transition pore (PTP) openings, followed by coenzyme A (CoA) release, acyl CoA synthesis, and membrane protein palmitoylation.
evidence: The abstract presents this as part of the pathway, supported by experimental data in Figure 3.

claim: MEND requires membrane protein palmitoylation.
source: We present evidence that MEND depends on mitochondrial permeability transition pore (PTP) openings, followed by coenzyme A (CoA) release, acyl CoA synthesis, and membrane protein palmitoylation.
evidence: The abstract presents this as part of the pathway, supported by experimental data in Figures 3 and 5.

claim: MEND is blocked by inhibiting mitochondrial Ca uptake.
source: MEND is blocked by inhibiting mitochondrial Ca uptake or PTP openings, depleting fatty acids, blocking acyl CoA synthesis, metabolizing CoA, or inhibiting palmitoylation.
evidence: The abstract states this as a finding, supported by experimental data in Figure 1B showing RU323 inhibition.

claim: MEND is blocked by inhibiting PTP openings.
source: MEND is blocked by inhibiting mitochondrial Ca uptake or PTP openings, depleting fatty acids, blocking acyl CoA synthesis, metabolizing CoA, or inhibiting palmitoylation.
evidence: The abstract states this as a finding, supported by experimental data in Figure 1B showing cyclosporine A and NIM811 inhibition.

claim: MEND is blocked by depleting fatty acids.
source: MEND is blocked by inhibiting mitochondrial Ca uptake or PTP openings, depleting fatty acids, blocking acyl CoA synthesis, metabolizing CoA, or inhibiting palmitoylation.
evidence: The abstract states this as a finding, supported by experimental data in Figure 3A showing fatty acid-free albumin effects.

claim: MEND is blocked by blocking acyl CoA synthesis.
source: MEND is blocked by inhibiting mitochondrial Ca uptake or PTP openings, depleting fatty acids, blocking acyl CoA synthesis, metabolizing CoA, or inhibiting palmitoylation.
evidence: The abstract states this as a finding, supported by experimental data in Figure 3A showing triacsin C inhibition.

claim: MEND is blocked by metabolizing CoA.
source: MEND is blocked by inhibiting mitochondrial Ca uptake or PTP openings, depleting fatty acids, blocking acyl CoA synthesis, metabolizing CoA, or inhibiting palmitoylation.
evidence: The abstract states this as a finding, supported by experimental data in Figure 3A showing acetyl CoA synthetase effects.

claim: MEND is blocked by inhibiting palmitoylation.
source: MEND is blocked by inhibiting mitochondrial Ca uptake or PTP openings, depleting fatty acids, blocking acyl CoA synthesis, metabolizing CoA, or inhibiting palmitoylation.
evidence: The abstract states this as a finding, supported by experimental data in Figure 3A showing bromopalmitate inhibition.

claim: MEND is triggered by depolarizing mitochondria.
source: It is triggered by depolarizing mitochondria or promoting PTP openings.
evidence: The abstract states this as a finding, supported by experimental data in Figure 1B showing CCCP and oligomycin effects.

claim: MEND is triggered by promoting PTP openings.
source: It is triggered by depolarizing mitochondria or promoting PTP openings.
evidence: The abstract states this as a finding, supported by experimental data in Figure 2 showing KSP solution effects.

claim: After mitochondrial MEND blockade, MEND is restored by cytoplasmic acyl CoA.
source: After mitochondrial MEND blockade, MEND is restored by cytoplasmic acyl CoA or CoA.
evidence: The abstract states this as a finding, supported by experimental data in Figure 4.

claim: After mitochondrial MEND blockade, MEND is restored by cytoplasmic CoA.
source: After mitochondrial MEND blockade, MEND is restored by cytoplasmic acyl CoA or CoA.
evidence: The abstract states this as a finding, supported by experimental data in Figure 4B.

claim: MEND is blocked by siRNA knockdown of the plasmalemmal acyl transferase, DHHC5.
source: MEND is blocked by siRNA knockdown of the plasmalemmal acyl transferase, DHHC5.
evidence: The abstract states this as a finding, supported by experimental data in Figure 5.

claim: When acyl CoA is abundant, transient H2O2 oxidative stress initiates MEND.
source: When acyl CoA is abundant, transient H2O2 oxidative stress or PKC activation initiates MEND, but the immediate presence of H2O2 prevents MEND.
evidence: The abstract states this as a finding, supported by experimental data in Figure 6B.

claim: When acyl CoA is abundant, PKC activation initiates MEND.
source: When acyl CoA is abundant, transient H2O2 oxidative stress or PKC activation initiates MEND, but the immediate presence of H2O2 prevents MEND.
evidence: The abstract states this as a finding, supported by experimental data in Figure 6A.

claim: The immediate presence of H2O2 prevents MEND.
source: When acyl CoA is abundant, transient H2O2 oxidative stress or PKC activation initiates MEND, but the immediate presence of H2O2 prevents MEND.
evidence: The abstract states this as a finding, supported by experimental data in Figure 6B showing inhibition during H2O2 application.

claim: The PTP inhibitor, NIM811, significantly increases plasmalemma in normally growing cells.
source: The PTP inhibitor, NIM811, significantly increases plasmalemma in normally growing cells.
evidence: The abstract states this as a finding, supported by experimental data in Figure 7.

claim: The MEND pathway may contribute to constitutive plasmalemma turnover in dependence on mitochondrial stress signaling.
source: Thus, the MEND pathway may contribute to constitutive as well as pathological plasmalemma turnover in dependence on mitochondrial stress signaling.
evidence: The abstract presents this as a conclusion based on the NIM811 data in Figure 7.

claim: The MEND pathway may contribute to pathological plasmalemma turnover in dependence on mitochondrial stress signaling.
source: Thus, the MEND pathway may contribute to constitutive as well as pathological plasmalemma turnover in dependence on mitochondrial stress signaling.
evidence: The abstract presents this as a conclusion based on the overall findings.

claim: Endocytic processes that do not use classical endocytic proteins remain poorly understood.
source: Endocytic processes that do not use classical endocytic proteins remain poorly understood because they are mechanistically inhomogeneous and difficult to study in isolation (Mayor and Pagano, 2007; Doherty and McMahon, 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Non-classical endocytic processes are mechanistically inhomogeneous and difficult to study in isolation.
source: Endocytic processes that do not use classical endocytic proteins remain poorly understood because they are mechanistically inhomogeneous and difficult to study in isolation (Mayor and Pagano, 2007; Doherty and McMahon, 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Non-classical endocytic processes are involved in cell migration.
source: Nevertheless, they are involved in a wide range of cellular processes, including cell migration (Howes et al., 2010), cell wounding responses (Tam et al., 2010), and pathogen internalization (Vidricaire and Tremblay, 2007), as well as membrane recycling in some neurons (Gong et al., 2008) and astrocytes (Jiang and Chen, 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Howes et al., 2010.

claim: Non-classical endocytic processes are involved in cell wounding responses.
source: Nevertheless, they are involved in a wide range of cellular processes, including cell migration (Howes et al., 2010), cell wounding responses (Tam et al., 2010), and pathogen internalization (Vidricaire and Tremblay, 2007), as well as membrane recycling in some neurons (Gong et al., 2008) and astrocytes (Jiang and Chen, 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Tam et al., 2010.

claim: Non-classical endocytic processes are involved in pathogen internalization.
source: Nevertheless, they are involved in a wide range of cellular processes, including cell migration (Howes et al., 2010), cell wounding responses (Tam et al., 2010), and pathogen internalization (Vidricaire and Tremblay, 2007), as well as membrane recycling in some neurons (Gong et al., 2008) and astrocytes (Jiang and Chen, 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Vidricaire and Tremblay, 2007.

claim: Non-classical endocytic processes are involved in membrane recycling in some neurons.
source: Nevertheless, they are involved in a wide range of cellular processes, including cell migration (Howes et al., 2010), cell wounding responses (Tam et al., 2010), and pathogen internalization (Vidricaire and Tremblay, 2007), as well as membrane recycling in some neurons (Gong et al., 2008) and astrocytes (Jiang and Chen, 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Gong et al., 2008.

claim: Non-classical endocytic processes are involved in membrane recycling in astrocytes.
source: Nevertheless, they are involved in a wide range of cellular processes, including cell migration (Howes et al., 2010), cell wounding responses (Tam et al., 2010), and pathogen internalization (Vidricaire and Tremblay, 2007), as well as membrane recycling in some neurons (Gong et al., 2008) and astrocytes (Jiang and Chen, 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Jiang and Chen, 2009.

claim: Massive endocytic (MEND) responses are the largest endocytic responses ever characterized.
source: Massive endocytic (MEND) responses described by us (Fine et al., 2011; Hilgemann and Fine, 2011; Lariccia et al., 2011) are the largest endocytic responses ever characterized.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to the authors' previous work.

claim: Large fractions of the plasmalemma that are internalized during MEND bind many amphipathic molecules less well than membrane remaining at the cell surface.
source: Large fractions of the plasmalemma that are internalized bind many amphipathic molecules less well than membrane remaining at the cell surface (Hilgemann and Fine, 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Hilgemann and Fine, 2011.

claim: MEND internalizes preferentially the more 'ordered' portions of the surface membrane.
source: Thus, MEND internalizes preferentially the more 'ordered' portions of the surface membrane.
evidence: This is inferred from the previous statement about amphipathic molecule binding.

claim: Different forms of MEND can be distinguished on the basis of ATP-, polyamine-, and Ca-dependence.
source: Different forms of MEND can be distinguished on the basis of ATP-, polyamine-, and Ca-dependence (Lariccia et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Lariccia et al., 2011.

claim: MEND can be initiated by rapidly cleaving sphingomyelin in the outer plasmalemma monolayer with bacterial sphingomyelinase C.
source: In addition, MEND can be initiated by rapidly cleaving sphingomyelin in the outer plasmalemma monolayer with bacterial sphingomyelinase C (Lariccia et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Lariccia et al., 2011.

claim: Native sphingomyelinases are translocated to the cell surface via exocytosis during cell wound responses.
source: It has been suggested that this form of MEND becomes activated during cell wound responses when native sphingomyelinases are translocated to the cell surface via exocytosis (Tam et al., 2010; Corrotte et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Tam et al., 2010 and Corrotte et al., 2013.

claim: ATP-dependent endocytic responses in BHK fibroblasts are functionally similar to 'excessive' endocytosis that occurs after large Ca transients in secretory cells.
source: These ATP-dependent endocytic responses are functionally similar to 'excessive' endocytosis that occurs after large Ca transients in secretory cells (Smith and Neher, 1997).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Smith and Neher, 1997.

claim: Up to 70% of the cell surface of fibroblasts can be internalized during MEND.
source: Up to 70% of the cell surface of fibroblasts can be internalized, followed by replenishment of the plasmalemma from internal membrane pools over 20 to 40 min (Lariccia et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Lariccia et al., 2011.

claim: The plasmalemma is replenished from internal membrane pools over 20 to 40 min after MEND.
source: Up to 70% of the cell surface of fibroblasts can be internalized, followed by replenishment of the plasmalemma from internal membrane pools over 20 to 40 min (Lariccia et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Lariccia et al., 2011.

claim: Ca transients act initially to prime mitochondria to open PTPs.
source: As described here, our data support the hypothesis that Ca transients act initially to prime mitochondria to open PTPs (permeability transition pore) (Giorgio et al., 2013), releasing metabolites to the cytoplasm (Azzolin et al., 2010).
evidence: This is presented as a hypothesis supported by the data, with citations to Giorgio et al., 2013 and Azzolin et al., 2010.

claim: PTP openings release metabolites to the cytoplasm.
source: As described here, our data support the hypothesis that Ca transients act initially to prime mitochondria to open PTPs (permeability transition pore) (Giorgio et al., 2013), releasing metabolites to the cytoplasm (Azzolin et al., 2010).
evidence: This is presented as a hypothesis supported by the data, with a citation to Azzolin et al., 2010.

claim: Palmitoylation of surface membrane proteins promotes the coalescence of ordered membrane domains by promoting protein clustering.
source: At the distal end of the pathway, our data suggest that palmitoylation of surface membrane proteins promotes the coalescence of ordered membrane domains by promoting protein clustering, as described biochemically (Levental et al., 2010) and as occurs in anoxia-related metabolic stress (Frank et al., 1980).
evidence: This is presented as a suggestion based on the data, with citations to Levental et al., 2010 and Frank et al., 1980.

claim: Protein clustering occurs in anoxia-related metabolic stress.
source: At the distal end of the pathway, our data suggest that palmitoylation of surface membrane proteins promotes the coalescence of ordered membrane domains by promoting protein clustering, as described biochemically (Levental et al., 2010) and as occurs in anoxia-related metabolic stress (Frank et al., 1980).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Frank et al., 1980.

claim: CoA is synthesized on the outer mitochondrial surface.
source: First, it is known that coenzyme A (CoA), which is synthesized on the outer mitochondrial surface, is accumulated into the matrix space by voltage-sensitive transporters (Tahiliani, 1991; Leonardi et al., 2005), generating CoA gradients to the cytoplasm of at least 50:1 (Tahiliani and Neely, 1987).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Tahiliani, 1991 and Leonardi et al., 2005.

claim: CoA is accumulated into the mitochondrial matrix space by voltage-sensitive transporters.
source: First, it is known that coenzyme A (CoA), which is synthesized on the outer mitochondrial surface, is accumulated into the matrix space by voltage-sensitive transporters (Tahiliani, 1991; Leonardi et al., 2005), generating CoA gradients to the cytoplasm of at least 50:1 (Tahiliani and Neely, 1987).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Tahiliani, 1991 and Leonardi et al., 2005.

claim: CoA gradients from mitochondria to the cytoplasm are at least 50:1.
source: First, it is known that coenzyme A (CoA), which is synthesized on the outer mitochondrial surface, is accumulated into the matrix space by voltage-sensitive transporters (Tahiliani, 1991; Leonardi et al., 2005), generating CoA gradients to the cytoplasm of at least 50:1 (Tahiliani and Neely, 1987).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Tahiliani and Neely, 1987.

claim: Transient openings of PTPs can release CoA and generate cytoplasmic CoA transients in the range of tens of micromolar without serious consequences for other mitochondrial metabolites.
source: Therefore, transient openings of nonselective mitochondrial pores, PTPs, can potentially release CoA and generate cytoplasmic CoA transients in the range of tens of micromolar without serious consequences for other mitochondrial metabolites.
evidence: This is inferred from the CoA gradient data and the nature of PTP openings.

claim: The low micromolar concentration of free CoA in the cytoplasm limits cytoplasmic acyl CoA synthetase activities.
source: Second, the low micromolar concentration of free CoA in the cytoplasm has long been suggested to limit cytoplasmic acyl CoA synthetase activities (Idell-Wenger et al., 1978), whereas free CoA is less likely to limit pyruvate dehydrogenases that have higher CoA affinities (Bremer, 1969).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Idell-Wenger et al., 1978.

claim: Free CoA is less likely to limit pyruvate dehydrogenases that have higher CoA affinities.
source: Second, the low micromolar concentration of free CoA in the cytoplasm has long been suggested to limit cytoplasmic acyl CoA synthetase activities (Idell-Wenger et al., 1978), whereas free CoA is less likely to limit pyruvate dehydrogenases that have higher CoA affinities (Bremer, 1969).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Bremer, 1969.

claim: Surface membrane proteins can cluster and decrease in number during anoxia and reoxygenation of cardiac tissue.
source: Third, it is known that surface membrane proteins, visualized as membrane particles in freeze fracture studies, can cluster and decrease in number (Frank et al., 1980) in a cellular circumstance known to cause PTP openings, namely during anoxia and reoxygenation of cardiac tissue (Brenner and Moulin, 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Frank et al., 1980 and Brenner and Moulin, 2012.

claim: Anoxia and reoxygenation of cardiac tissue causes PTP openings.
source: Third, it is known that surface membrane proteins, visualized as membrane particles in freeze fracture studies, can cluster and decrease in number (Frank et al., 1980) in a cellular circumstance known to cause PTP openings, namely during anoxia and reoxygenation of cardiac tissue (Brenner and Moulin, 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Brenner and Moulin, 2012.

claim: Mitochondria might control palmitoylation of membrane proteins in response to metabolic stress by releasing CoA to the cytoplasm.
source: Therewith, a working hypothesis is suggested that mitochondria might control palmitoylation of membrane proteins in response to metabolic stress by releasing CoA to the cytoplasm.
evidence: This is presented as a working hypothesis based on the cited literature.

claim: CoA release from mitochondria may occur via PTP openings.
source: In principle, this release may occur not only via PTP openings, but by reverse CoA transport during mitochondrial depolarization caused by partial PTP openings, and via membrane defects that might occur during mitochondrial fission and fusion events in metabolic stress (Knott et al., 2008; Ong et al., 2010; Frank et al., 2012).
evidence: This is presented as a possibility based on the working hypothesis.

claim: CoA release from mitochondria may occur by reverse CoA transport during mitochondrial depolarization caused by partial PTP openings.
source: In principle, this release may occur not only via PTP openings, but by reverse CoA transport during mitochondrial depolarization caused by partial PTP openings, and via membrane defects that might occur during mitochondrial fission and fusion events in metabolic stress (Knott et al., 2008; Ong et al., 2010; Frank et al., 2012).
evidence: This is presented as a possibility based on the working hypothesis.

claim: CoA release from mitochondria may occur via membrane defects during mitochondrial fission and fusion events in metabolic stress.
source: In principle, this release may occur not only via PTP openings, but by reverse CoA transport during mitochondrial depolarization caused by partial PTP openings, and via membrane defects that might occur during mitochondrial fission and fusion events in metabolic stress (Knott et al., 2008; Ong et al., 2010; Frank et al., 2012).
evidence: This is presented as a possibility based on the working hypothesis, with citations to Knott et al., 2008; Ong et al., 2010; Frank et al., 2012.

claim: Transient PTP openings occur physiologically, causing transient mitochondrial depolarizations accompanied by superoxide flashes.
source: It is now well established that transient PTP openings occur physiologically, causing transient mitochondrial depolarizations accompanied by superoxide flashes (Hausenloy et al., 2004; Saotome et al., 2009; Zhang et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Hausenloy et al., 2004; Saotome et al., 2009; Zhang et al., 2013.

claim: Low conductance PTP openings cause mitochondrial depolarization without loss of metabolites.
source: One widely-held view is that low conductance PTP openings cause mitochondrial depolarization without loss of metabolites, and thereby release excess mitochondrial Ca to the cytoplasm (Huser and Blatter, 1999; Korge et al., 2011; Zhou and O'Rourke, 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Huser and Blatter, 1999; Korge et al., 2011; Zhou and O'Rourke, 2012.

claim: It is possible for mitochondria to release metabolites by transient PTP openings without loss of mitochondrial membrane integrity or global mitochondrial depolarization.
source: Nevertheless, it appears possible for mitochondria to release metabolites by transient PTP openings without loss of mitochondrial membrane integrity or even global mitochondrial depolarization (Dumas et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Dumas et al., 2009.

claim: Knockout of cyclophilin D gives rise to hearts that are mildly protected from ischemia/reperfusion damage.
source: Knockout of cyclophilin D, a major PTP regulator (Basso et al., 2005), gives rise to intriguing phenotypes: hearts are mildly protected from ischemia/reperfusion damage, but animals are markedly less tolerant of physical exertion (swimming) and shift their energy metabolism from fatty acids to glucose (Elrod et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Basso et al., 2005 and Elrod et al., 2010.

claim: Knockout of cyclophilin D results in animals that are markedly less tolerant of physical exertion.
source: Knockout of cyclophilin D, a major PTP regulator (Basso et al., 2005), gives rise to intriguing phenotypes: hearts are mildly protected from ischemia/reperfusion damage, but animals are markedly less tolerant of physical exertion (swimming) and shift their energy metabolism from fatty acids to glucose (Elrod et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Elrod et al., 2010.

claim: Knockout of cyclophilin D results in animals that shift their energy metabolism from fatty acids to glucose.
source: Knockout of cyclophilin D, a major PTP regulator (Basso et al., 2005), gives rise to intriguing phenotypes: hearts are mildly protected from ischemia/reperfusion damage, but animals are markedly less tolerant of physical exertion (swimming) and shift their energy metabolism from fatty acids to glucose (Elrod et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Elrod et al., 2010.

claim: Cyclophilin D is a major PTP regulator.
source: Knockout of cyclophilin D, a major PTP regulator (Basso et al., 2005), gives rise to intriguing phenotypes: hearts are mildly protected from ischemia/reperfusion damage, but animals are markedly less tolerant of physical exertion (swimming) and shift their energy metabolism from fatty acids to glucose (Elrod et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Basso et al., 2005.

claim: Loss of mitochondrial depolarizations favors CoA accumulation by mitochondria and causes a decrease of cytoplasmic free CoA.
source: Our working hypothesis predicts that loss of mitochondrial depolarizations will also favor CoA accumulation by mitochondria and cause a decrease of cytoplasmic free CoA.
evidence: This is presented as a prediction from the working hypothesis.

claim: A lower cytoplasmic free CoA concentration might cause a shift from fatty acid to glucose metabolism, owing to the different CoA affinities of acyl CoA synthetases and pyruvate dehydrogenases.
source: Consequences of a lower cytoplasmic free CoA concentration might include the shift from fatty acid to glucose metabolism, owing to the different CoA affinities of acyl CoA synthetases and pyruvate dehydrogenases noted above.
evidence: This is presented as a speculative consequence based on the working hypothesis and previously cited CoA affinity differences.

claim: Plasmalemma surface area is monitored as membrane electrical capacitance (Cm) via patch clamp of BHK cells that express cardiac Na/Ca exchangers, NCX1.
source: Plasmalemma surface area is monitored as membrane electrical capacitance (Cm) via patch clamp of BHK cells that express cardiac Na/Ca exchangers, NCX1 (Linck et al., 1998).
evidence: This describes the experimental method used, with a citation to Linck et al., 1998.

claim: Potassium-free solutions are employed to block clathrin-dependent endocytosis.
source: Potassium-free solutions are employed to block clathrin-dependent endocytosis (Altankov and Grinnell, 1995) and to minimize membrane conductance.
evidence: This describes the experimental method used, with a citation to Altankov and Grinnell, 1995.

claim: During Ca influx, membrane area increases by 30% as a result of exocytosis in the Standard MEND protocol.
source: During Ca influx, outward membrane current reflects 3Na/1 Ca exchange. Membrane area (i.e., Cm) increases by 30% as a result of exocytosis (i.e., fusion of vesicles to the cell surface).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1A and described in the text.

claim: After terminating Ca influx, membrane area is stable for nearly 60 s and then declines over 2 min by 70% as plasmalemma is internalized via endocytosis.
source: After terminating Ca influx, membrane area is stable for nearly 60 s and then declines over 2 min by 70% as plasmalemma is internalized via endocytosis.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1A and described in the text.

claim: Removal of inorganic phosphate (Pi, 1 mM) from the standard cytoplasmic solution reduces MEND responses to less than 30% of peak membrane area.
source: The second bar set (purple) shows that removal of inorganic phosphate (Pi, 1 mM) from the standard cytoplasmic solution reduces MEND responses to less than 30% of peak membrane area, as expected from the activating effect of Pi on PTPs (Massari, 1996).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1B and described in the text, with a citation to Massari, 1996.

claim: The mitochondrial Ca uniporter inhibitor, RU323 (15 μM), strongly blocks MEND.
source: The third data set (blue) shows that the mitochondrial Ca uniporter inhibitor, RU323 (Ying et al., 1991) (15 μM), strongly blocks MEND.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1B and described in the text, with a citation to Ying et al., 1991.

claim: The nonspecific PTP inhibitor, cyclosporine A (CsA, 5 μM), strongly inhibits MEND.
source: Subsequently, it is shown that the nonspecific PTP inhibitor, cyclosporine A (Crompton et al., 1988) (CsA, 5 μM in cytoplasmic and extracellular solutions; green) and the PTP/cyclophilin D-specific cyclosporine, NIM811 (N-methyl-4-isoleucine cyclosporine) (2 μM; orange) (Waldmeier et al., 2002), also strongly inhibit MEND.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1B and described in the text, with citations to Crompton et al., 1988 and Waldmeier et al., 2002.

claim: The PTP/cyclophilin D-specific cyclosporine, NIM811 (2 μM), strongly inhibits MEND.
source: Subsequently, it is shown that the nonspecific PTP inhibitor, cyclosporine A (Crompton et al., 1988) (CsA, 5 μM in cytoplasmic and extracellular solutions; green) and the PTP/cyclophilin D-specific cyclosporine, NIM811 (N-methyl-4-isoleucine cyclosporine) (2 μM; orange) (Waldmeier et al., 2002), also strongly inhibit MEND.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1B and described in the text, with a citation to Waldmeier et al., 2002.

claim: The calcineurin inhibitor, FK506, had no effect on MEND, even at a high concentration.
source: Importantly, the calcineurin inhibitor, FK506, had no effect on MEND, even at a high concentration (Lariccia et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the text with a citation to Lariccia et al., 2011.

claim: Activation of protein kinase C epsilon (PKCε) protects cells from oxidative damage by inhibiting PTP openings.
source: Activation of protein kinase C epsilon (PKCε) is reported to protect cells from oxidative damage by inhibiting PTP openings (Baines et al., 2003; Budas and Mochly-Rosen, 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Baines et al., 2003 and Budas and Mochly-Rosen, 2007.

claim: Incubation with a PKC activator, OAG (15 μM), for 20 min before experiments effectively blocks Standard MEND.
source: Therefore, we incubated cells with a PKC activator, 1-oleoyl-2-acetyl-sn-glycerol (OAG, 15 μM), for 20 min before experiments, and Standard MEND was effectively blocked (yellow).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1B and described in the text.

claim: Rapid mitochondrial depolarization with CCCP (20 μM) and oligomycin (5 μM) causes cells to undergo 30% MEND responses within 1 min after rupturing the membrane in the patch pipette.
source: As indicated by the solid red bar graph for data point '1' (before the Ca transient), cells underwent 30% MEND responses within 1 min after rupturing the membrane in the patch pipette (i.e., 'opening' the cell to the patch pipette).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1B and described in the text.

claim: After rapid mitochondrial depolarization with CCCP and oligomycin, Ca influx initiates supernormal exocytic responses, but MEND is fully suppressed.
source: Thereafter, Ca influx initiated supernormal exocytic responses, from point '1' (before) to '2' (peak), but MEND was fully suppressed.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1B and described in the text.

claim: Rapid mitochondrial depolarization causes cells to be refractory to MEND for the duration of patch clamp experiments (∼30 min).
source: Thus, while rapid mitochondrial depolarization with these agents can activate single MEND responses with very little delay, cells subsequently are refractory to MEND for the duration of patch clamp experiments (∼30 min).
evidence: This is stated in the text based on the experimental observations.

claim: Mito-Tempo (10 μM) reduces average MEND responses from 42 ± 7% to 27 ± 6%, but the difference is not significant.
source: We report lastly in this connection an experiment set in which we tested for inhibition of MEND by an antioxidant that becomes targeted to mitochondria, Mito-Tempo (Jiang et al., 2009). When included in the pipette solution at 10 μM, average MEND responses were reduced from 42 ± 7% (n = 10) to 27 ± 6% (n = 8), but the difference was not significant.
evidence: This is stated in the text with a citation to Jiang et al., 2009.

claim: Cytoplasmic perfusion of KSP solution causes MEND responses over a time course of somewhat less than 1 min, amounting to 34 ± 6% of initial cell area at 37°C.
source: After a delay of several seconds, MEND responses occurred over a time course of somewhat less that 1 min and amounted to 34 ± 6% of initial cell area at 37°C.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2A and described in the text.

claim: The same KSP perfusion protocol induces no response at 22°C.
source: As shown by the lower trace in Figure 2A, the same protocol induced no response at 22°C.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2A and described in the text.

claim: Standard MEND responses at 37°C are negligible in cells that were initially opened at 22°C with KSP solution in the pipette.
source: Nevertheless, Figure 2B shows that Standard MEND responses at 37°C were negligible in cells that were initially opened at 22°C with KSP solution (potassium/succinate/phosphate-containing solution) in the pipette.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2B and described in the text.

claim: KSP solution induces a MEND-refractory state within at most 1 min, even when no MEND occurs at 22°C.
source: Thus, KSP solution, like mitochondrial depolarization, induces a MEND-refractory state within at most 1 min, even when no MEND occurs at 22°C.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental observations in Figure 2.

claim: Metabolites required for MEND might be released and lost into the patch pipette during cytoplasmic application of KSP solution.
source: Given that cytoplasmic solutes exchange with pipette solutions within a few seconds, this result suggests that metabolites required for MEND might be released and lost into the patch pipette during cytoplasmic application of KSP solution.
evidence: This is presented as a suggestion based on the experimental observations.

claim: Standard MEND is normal in cells that were incubated for 1 hr with 1:1 palmitate-loaded albumin (50 μM).
source: The first data set (black and white) shows that Standard MEND is normal in cells that were incubated for 1 hr with 1:1 palmitate-loaded albumin (50 μM; 'Alb+FA').
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3A and described in the text.

claim: Cyclosporine A (3 μM) blocks MEND, but perfusion of myristoyl CoA (15 μM) into cells causes MEND to occur within seconds.

Ca influx caused a 35% exocytic response, as usual, and membrane area (Cm ) was then stable until mCoA (15 μM) was perfused into the cell. Within seconds, membrane area began to fall, and within 2 min nearly 70% of the cell surface was removed by endocytosis.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4A and described in the text.

claim: Perfusion of myristoyl CoA (15 μM) overcomes MEND block by cyclosporine A.
source: Figure 4B shows composite data for mCoA release of MEND block by cyclosporine A (black and white), followed by results for release of MEND block by CCCP and oligomycin (purple), KSP-induced MEND block (blue), and OAG-induced MEND block (green).

claim: Perfusion of myristoyl CoA (15 μM) overcomes MEND block by CCCP and oligomycin.

claim: Perfusion of myristoyl CoA (15 μM) overcomes OAG-induced MEND block.

claim: MEND block by a high concentration of CoA (3 mM) is immediately relieved by its washout from cells.

evidence: This is shown in Figure 4B and described in the text.

claim: DHHC2 and DHHC5 are the only DHHC transferases known to traffic to and become active at the plasmalemma.
source: From more than 20 DHHC transferases (Mitchell et al., 2006) only DHHC2 and DHHC5 are known at this time to traffic to and become active at the plasmalemma (Greaves et al., 2011; Li et al., 2011; Thomas et al., 2012), and DHHC5 may be more ubiquitous (Li et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Mitchell et al., 2006; Greaves et al., 2011; Li et al., 2011; Thomas et al., 2012.

claim: DHHC5 may be more ubiquitous than DHHC2.
source: From more than 20 DHHC transferases (Mitchell et al., 2006) only DHHC2 and DHHC5 are known at this time to traffic to and become active at the plasmalemma (Greaves et al., 2011; Li et al., 2011; Thomas et al., 2012), and DHHC5 may be more ubiquitous (Li et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Li et al., 2011.

claim: DHHC5 expression was decreased by >80% in BHK cells using siRNA with lipofectamine2000 transfection.
source: Using siRNA for DHHC5 with lipofectamine2000 transfection, Figure 5A documents in Western blots that DHHC5 expression was decreased by >80% in BHK cells.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5A and described in the text.

claim: Incubating BHK cells during the entire siRNA protocol with a low concentration of staurosporine (STS, 0.1 μM) generates larger MEND responses.
source: We were able to overcome this variability and generate even larger MEND responses by incubating BHK cells during the entire siRNA protocol with a low concentration of a PKC inhibitor, staurosporine (STS, 0.1 μM), that prevents PKC-induced inhibition of PTPs (Ytrehus et al., 1994).
evidence: This is stated in the text with a citation to Ytrehus et al., 1994.

claim: Staurosporine (0.1 μM) prevents PKC-induced inhibition of PTPs.
source: We were able to overcome this variability and generate even larger MEND responses by incubating BHK cells during the entire siRNA protocol with a low concentration of a PKC inhibitor, staurosporine (STS, 0.1 μM), that prevents PKC-induced inhibition of PTPs (Ytrehus et al., 1994).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Ytrehus et al., 1994.

claim: In control transfected cells grown with staurosporine, exocytic responses are larger than normal, and subsequent MEND responses remove fully 75% of the cell surface.
source: As shown in Figure 5B using LF2000 to transfect cells, exocytic responses in control transfected cells were larger than normal, and subsequent MEND responses removed fully 75% of the cell surface.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5B and described in the text.

claim: In cells transfected with siRNA for DHHC5, MEND responses are decreased on average to 25% of the cell surface, corresponding to a 66% decrease of the MEND response.
source: In cells transfected with siRNA for DHHC5 (right data set in Figure 5B), these MEND responses were decreased on average to 25% of the cell surface, corresponding to a 66% decrease of the MEND response.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5B and described in the text.

claim: siRNA of DHHC5 strongly blocks MEND responses induced by pipette perfusion of mCoA into cells that were MEND-blocked by cyclosporine A (3 μM).

evidence: This is shown in Figure 5C and described in the text.

claim: KSP-induced MEND in cells transfected with scrambled DHHC5 siRNA amounts to only 14%.
source: Figure 5D quantifies KSP-induced MEND in BHK cells that were not STS-treated. Accordingly, KSP-induced MEND in cells transfected with scrambled DHHC5 siRNA amounts to only 14%.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5D and described in the text.

claim: KSP-induced MEND is highly significantly reduced to 2.5% by DHHC5 siRNA transfection.
source: Nevertheless, the responses were reproducible, and they were highly significantly reduced to 2.5% by DHHC5 siRNA transfection.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5D and described in the text.

claim: The introduction of acyl CoA (mCoA) into cells is not sufficient to initiate MEND under standard conditions.
source: As shown in Figure 6A, however, the introduction of acyl CoA (mCoA) into cells is not sufficient to initiate MEND. Under standard conditions, cytoplasmic perfusion of mCoA (15 μM) causes only 5 to, at most, 10% endocytic responses over 10 min (n > 20; green square in Figure 6A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6A and described in the text.

claim: Cytoplasmic perfusion of mCoA (15 μM) causes only 5 to, at most, 10% endocytic responses over 10 min under standard conditions.
source: Under standard conditions, cytoplasmic perfusion of mCoA (15 μM) causes only 5 to, at most, 10% endocytic responses over 10 min (n > 20; green square in Figure 6A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6A and described in the text.

claim: Activation of PKCs can promote MEND in the presence of acyl CoA and in the absence of Ca transients.
source: From many possibilities, we describe in Figure 6 that two common Ca-dependent cell signals, activation of PKCs and generation of reactive oxygen (ROS), both can promote MEND in the presence of acyl CoA and in the absence of Ca transients.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 6.

claim: Generation of reactive oxygen (ROS) can promote MEND in the presence of acyl CoA and in the absence of Ca transients.
source: From many possibilities, we describe in Figure 6 that two common Ca-dependent cell signals, activation of PKCs and generation of reactive oxygen (ROS), both can promote MEND in the presence of acyl CoA and in the absence of Ca transients.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 6.

claim: Application of OAG (15 μM) for 1 to 2 min has little or no effect on endocytosis in the absence of mCoA.
source: Extracellular application of OAG (15 μM) for 1 to 2 min also has little or no effect, even after 6 min.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6A and described in the text.

claim: With mCoA (15 μM) in the cytoplasmic solution, OAG initiates a decrease of membrane area that continues for several minutes after OAG is removed, amounting to 24% on average after 6 min.
source: With mCoA (15 μM) in the cytoplsamic solution, OAG initiates a decrease of membrane area that continues for several minutes after OAG is removed, amounting to 24% on average after 6 min.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6A and described in the text.

claim: Application of H2O2 (80 μM) for 4 min has little or no effect over 15 min in the absence of mCoA.
source: Application of H2O2 (80 μM) for 4 min has little or no effect over 15 min in the absence of mCoA.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6B and described in the text.

claim: With mCoA (15 μM) in the cytoplasmic solution, application of H2O2 causes little or no change initially, but upon its removal membrane area begins to decline robustly within 1 min and on average more than 25% of the cell surface is lost over 10 min.
source: In the presence of mCoA (15 μM), application of H2O2 causes little or no change initially, but upon its removal membrane area begins to decline robustly within 1 min and on average more than 25% of the cell surface is lost over 10 min.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6B and described in the text.

claim: ROS have an acute inhibitory effect on MEND, which is rapidly relieved when H2O2 is removed.
source: This pattern suggests that ROS have an acute inhibitory effect on MEND, which is rapidly relieved when H2O2 is removed.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental observations in Figure 6B.

claim: The stimulatory effect of ROS on MEND is a long-lived effect.
source: The stimulatory effect of ROS on MEND, however, is a long-lived effect.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental observations in Figure 6B.

claim: Transient generation of ROS during the MEND protocol promotes the final steps of MEND, subsequent to generation of acyl CoA.
source: The results suggest that transient generation of ROS during the MEND protocol promotes the final steps of MEND, subsequent to generation of acyl CoA.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental observations in Figure 6.

claim: MEND responses promoted by OAG are strongly inhibited by a peptide substrate inhibitor of conventional PKCs (PKC peptide (19–36), 1 μM).
source: MEND responses promoted by OAG are strongly inhibited by a peptide substrate inhibitor of conventional PKCs (PKC peptide (19–36), 1 μM), confirming that conventional PKCs are involved (House and Kemp, 1987).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6C and described in the text, with a citation to House and Kemp, 1987.

claim: The induction of MEND by H2O2 is not inhibited by the PKC peptide.
source: By contrast, the induction of MEND by H2O2 is not inhibited by the PKC peptide, indicating that H2O2 is not acting through the PKCs that can promote MEND.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6C and described in the text.

claim: H2O2 is not acting through the PKCs that can promote MEND.
source: By contrast, the induction of MEND by H2O2 is not inhibited by the PKC peptide, indicating that H2O2 is not acting through the PKCs that can promote MEND.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of PKC peptide inhibition of H2O2-induced MEND.

claim: MEND activation by H2O2 and OAG are not additive.
source: Finally, we show that MEND activation by H2O2 and OAG are not additive; the activation of MEND by one reagent precludes a further effect by the other.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6C and described in the text.

claim: Phosphorylation of some DHHC protein substrates by PKCs can be permissive for their subsequent palmitoylation.
source: However, one possibility raised by the literature is that phosphorylation of some DHHC protein substrates by PKCs can be permissive for their subsequent palmitoylation.
evidence: This is presented as a possibility based on the literature.

source: This is the case for the dually palmitoylated, Na/K pump regulatory protein, phospholemman (PLM) (Tulloch et al., 2011), which is expressed preferentially in muscle (Geering, 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Tulloch et al., 2011 and Geering, 2006.

claim: Phospholemman (PLM) is expressed preferentially in muscle.
source: This is the case for the dually palmitoylated, Na/K pump regulatory protein, phospholemman (PLM) (Tulloch et al., 2011), which is expressed preferentially in muscle (Geering, 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Geering, 2006.

claim: Overexpression of PLM causes a three-fold increase in the rate of PKC/mCoA-dependent MEND.
source: The overexpression of PLM caused a three-fold increase in the rate of PKC/mCoA-dependent MEND.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6D and described in the text.

claim: MEND can be promoted by the presence of proteins that can be palmitoylated and therefore is a 'cargo-dependent' form of endocytosis.
source: This result clearly supports the idea that MEND can be promoted by the presence of proteins that can be palmitoylated and therefore is a 'cargo-dependent' form of endocytosis.
evidence: This is inferred from the PLM overexpression data in Figure 6D.

claim: Treatment of BHK cells with NIM811 (2 μM) causes a significant increase of membrane area after a delay of 1 hr, reaching a plateau within about 3 hr.
source: In summary, treatment of BHK cells with NIM811 causes a significant increase of membrane area after a delay of 1 hr, reaching a plateau within about 3 hr, indicating 'either' that membrane insertion at the cell surface is increased 'or' that membrane removal from the cell surface is decreased, as expected for partial inhibition of endocytosis.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7B and described in the text.

claim: Membrane area in cells grown with NIM811 (2 μM) for 28 hr is increased on average by 27% compared to control cells of equal size.
source: In the second set of experiments, we grew BHK cells normally for 28 hr in the presence of NIM811 (2 μM) and carried out equivalent measurements after removing cells from dishes. Membrane area in cells of equal size was increased on average by 27% (p<0.01).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7B and described in the text.

claim: Treatment of BHK cells with NIM811 indicates that either membrane insertion at the cell surface is increased or membrane removal from the cell surface is decreased.
source: In summary, treatment of BHK cells with NIM811 causes a significant increase of membrane area after a delay of 1 hr, reaching a plateau within about 3 hr, indicating 'either' that membrane insertion at the cell surface is increased 'or' that membrane removal from the cell surface is decreased, as expected for partial inhibition of endocytosis.
evidence: This is inferred from the NIM811 data in Figure 7.

claim: Ca-dependent endocytosis in BHK fibroblasts occurs by unconventional mechanisms.
source: Patch clamp techniques allow extensive manipulation of single cells, and we have exploited those possibilities to analyze Ca-dependent endocytosis that occurs in BHK fibroblasts by unconventional mechanisms (Lariccia et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Lariccia et al., 2011.

claim: Transient openings of mitochondrial PTPs rapidly release CoA from the mitochondrial matrix space to the cytoplasm.
source: In spite of clear limitations, we argue that our data sets support working hypotheses summarized in Figure 8: transient openings of mitochondrial PTPs, which can be inhibited by the activation of PKCε (Baines et al., 2003), rapidly release CoA from the mitochondrial matrix space to the cytoplasm.
evidence: This is presented as a working hypothesis supported by the data, with a citation to Baines et al., 2003.

claim: Generation of cytoplasmic acyl CoA promotes membrane protein palmitoylation via the DHHC5 acyl transferase.
source: Then, generation of cytoplasmic acyl CoA promotes membrane protein palmitoylation via the DHHC5 acyl transferase.
evidence: This is presented as a working hypothesis supported by the data.

claim: Palmitoylation promotes membrane protein clustering.
source: We hypothesize that palmitolyation promotes membrane protein clustering (Levental et al., 2010) and that clustering beyond a threshold promotes budding and internalization of Lo membrane domains (Fine et al., 2011; Hilgemann and Fine, 2011; Lariccia et al., 2011).
evidence: This is presented as a hypothesis with citations to Levental et al., 2010; Fine et al., 2011; Hilgemann and Fine, 2011; Lariccia et al., 2011.

claim: Clustering of membrane proteins beyond a threshold promotes budding and internalization of Lo membrane domains.
source: We hypothesize that palmitolyation promotes membrane protein clustering (Levental et al., 2010) and that clustering beyond a threshold promotes budding and internalization of Lo membrane domains (Fine et al., 2011; Hilgemann and Fine, 2011; Lariccia et al., 2011).
evidence: This is presented as a hypothesis with citations to Fine et al., 2011; Hilgemann and Fine, 2011; Lariccia et al., 2011.

claim: Conventional PKC activation increases the availability of sites for palmitoylation.
source: We speculate that conventional PKC activation and 'transient' H2O2 stress promote MEND progression by increasing the availability of sites for palmitoylation, whereas the immediate presence of oxidative stress inhibits MEND progression by inhibiting palmitoylation reactions.
evidence: This is presented as speculation based on the data.

claim: Transient H2O2 stress promotes MEND progression by increasing the availability of sites for palmitoylation.
source: We speculate that conventional PKC activation and 'transient' H2O2 stress promote MEND progression by increasing the availability of sites for palmitoylation, whereas the immediate presence of oxidative stress inhibits MEND progression by inhibiting palmitoylation reactions.
evidence: This is presented as speculation based on the data.

claim: The immediate presence of oxidative stress inhibits MEND progression by inhibiting palmitoylation reactions.
source: We speculate that conventional PKC activation and 'transient' H2O2 stress promote MEND progression by increasing the availability of sites for palmitoylation, whereas the immediate presence of oxidative stress inhibits MEND progression by inhibiting palmitoylation reactions.
evidence: This is presented as speculation based on the data.

claim: PIP2 must be resynthesized after its depletion during Ca transients for MEND to occur.
source: We have shown previously that PIP2 must be resynthesized after its depletion during Ca transients (Lariccia et al., 2011), but we do not know what specific role phosophoinositide turnover plays.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Lariccia et al., 2011.

claim: Constitutive endocytosis in BHK cells internalizes between one and two percent of the surface membrane per min, mostly via well-defined coated pits.
source: Constitutive endocytosis in BHK cells has been analyzed rather extensively (Marsh and Helenius, 1980; Griffiths et al., 1989). Between one and two percent of the surface membrane is internalized per min, mostly via well-defined coated pits (Marsh and Helenius, 1980).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Marsh and Helenius, 1980 and Griffiths et al., 1989.

claim: Endocytic mechanisms that internalize 'lipid raft' proteins, in particular GPI-anchored proteins, are well characterized in BHK cells.
source: Certainly, endocytic mechanisms that internalize 'lipid raft' proteins, in particular GPI-anchored proteins (Lakhan et al., 2009), are also well characterized in BHK cells (Fivaz et al., 2002; Refaei et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Lakhan et al., 2009; Fivaz et al., 2002; Refaei et al., 2011.

claim: The mechanisms underlying MEND may be constitutively active, possibly in dependence on spontaneous mitochondrial depolarizations and superoxide flashes.
source: It therefore cannot be discounted that the mechanisms underlying MEND are constitutively active, possibly in dependence on spontaneous mitochondrial depolarizations and superoxide flashes (Elrod et al., 2010; Zhang et al., 2013) and consistent with the increase of sarcolemma area caused by NIM811 (Figure 7).
evidence: This is presented as a possibility based on the data and citations to Elrod et al., 2010 and Zhang et al., 2013.

claim: MEND can internalize surface membrane at a rate of 50% per min, at least 25-times greater than constitutive membrane turnover.
source: MEND can internalize surface membrane at a rate of 50% per min (Figure 1), at least 25-times greater than constitutive membrane turnover.
evidence: This is stated in the text based on the data in Figure 1.

claim: A constitutive activity of the MEND pathway equal to even one percent of its maximal activity would be a substantial endocytic flux in BHK cells.
source: Therefore, a constitutive activity of the MEND pathway equal to even one percent of its maximal activity would be a substantial endocytic flux in BHK cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of MEND and constitutive endocytosis rates.

claim: DHHC5 is constitutively functional in cells.
source: Clearly, DHHC5 is constitutively functional in cells (Li et al., 2011; Thomas et al., 2012), and both PKC activation and H2O2 promote acyl CoA-dependent endocytosis without the activation of Ca transients (Figure 6).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Li et al., 2011 and Thomas et al., 2012.

claim: Both PKC activation and H2O2 promote acyl CoA-dependent endocytosis without the activation of Ca transients.
source: Clearly, DHHC5 is constitutively functional in cells (Li et al., 2011; Thomas et al., 2012), and both PKC activation and H2O2 promote acyl CoA-dependent endocytosis without the activation of Ca transients (Figure 6).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6 and described in the text.

claim: Endocytosis following PKC activation might reflect the endocytic process that normally inactivates PKCs by removing PKCs from the cell surface.
source: Endocytosis following PKC activation might in principle reflect the endocyotic process that normally inactivates PKCs by removing PKCs from the cell surface (Carmena and Sardini, 2007).
evidence: This is presented as a possibility with a citation to Carmena and Sardini, 2007.

claim: A 'caveolar' or 'lipid raft' pathway that is blocked by nystatin participates in PKC inactivation.
source: Although generally ascribed to conventional, ubiquitin-dependent endocytosis, a 'caveolar' or 'lipid raft' pathway that is blocked by nystatin has also been shown to participate in PKC inactivation (Leontieva and Black, 2004).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Leontieva and Black, 2004.

claim: PLM appears to be palmitoylated in dependence on its phosphorylation by PKCs.
source: PLM appears to be palmitoylated in dependence on its phosphorylation by PKCs (Tulloch et al., 2011), and expression of PLM promotes acyl CoA/PKC-dependent endocytosis (Figure 6).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Tulloch et al., 2011.

claim: Expression of PLM promotes acyl CoA/PKC-dependent endocytosis.
source: PLM appears to be palmitoylated in dependence on its phosphorylation by PKCs (Tulloch et al., 2011), and expression of PLM promotes acyl CoA/PKC-dependent endocytosis (Figure 6).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6D and described in the text.

claim: Mitochondrial signaling impacts the plasmalemma by controlling and/or modulating surface membrane protein palmitoylation and subsequently palmitoylation-dependent endocytosis.
source: In summary, our work lends support to a working hypothesis that mitochondrial signaling impacts the plasmalemma by controlling and/or modulating surface membrane protein palmitoylation and subsequently palmitoylation-dependent endocytosis.
evidence: This is presented as a summary of the working hypothesis supported by the data.

claim: One trigger for mitochondrial signaling to the plasmalemma appears to be release of CoA from mitochondria during mitochondrial depolarizations that involve transient PTP openings.
source: One trigger appears to be release of CoA from mitochondria during mitochondrial depolarizations that involve transient PTP openings (Huser and Blatter, 1999; Korge et al., 2011).
evidence: This is presented as a conclusion based on the data, with citations to Huser and Blatter, 1999 and Korge et al., 2011.

claim: Activation of PKCs prior to a Ca transient blocks MEND.
source: Activation of PKCs prior to a Ca transient blocks MEND, while both PKCs and transient generation of ROS support MEND progression at the cell surface.
evidence: This is stated in the text based on the experimental observations.

claim: Both PKCs and transient generation of ROS support MEND progression at the cell surface.
source: Activation of PKCs prior to a Ca transient blocks MEND, while both PKCs and transient generation of ROS support MEND progression at the cell surface.
evidence: This is stated in the text based on the experimental observations.

claim: A wave of PKC activation during MEND will tend to restabilize mitochondria but promote ongoing endocytic events.
source: Accordingly, a wave of PKC activation during MEND will tend to restabilize mitochondria but promote ongoing endocytic events.
evidence: This is presented as a conclusion based on the data and the working hypothesis.

claim: MEND is related to Ca-activated excessive endocytosis in secretory cells.
source: It will be of great interest to establish how and if the MEND pathway is related to Ca-activated excessive endocytosis (Smith and Neher, 1997) and bulk endocytosis (Cousin, 2009) in secretory cells.
evidence: This is presented as a question for future research, with citations to Smith and Neher, 1997 and Cousin, 2009.

claim: MEND is related to bulk endocytosis in secretory cells.
source: It will be of great interest to establish how and if the MEND pathway is related to Ca-activated excessive endocytosis (Smith and Neher, 1997) and bulk endocytosis (Cousin, 2009) in secretory cells.
evidence: This is presented as a question for future research, with a citation to Cousin, 2009.
